extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; historians of American press; journalists interested in historical newspaper practices
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes criteria and standards implied or stated in a historical account of U.S. newspapers (c.1833–1860) about how papers were produced, organized, and judged — covering editorial style, format, distribution, economics, and newsgathering practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial tone / civility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Another characteristic of the Times was its self-possessed good manners. It had strong opinions, and it was fond of controversy; but it never descended, as Greeley sometimes did, to billings-gate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measured, civil, self-possessed editorial voice even when taking strong positions; avoid personal abuse and coarse invective (billings-gate). The Times was modeled on the London Times as an example of this restrained tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: News balance and comprehensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Its news was well balanced, well edited, and copious, with special attention to foreign affairs; thus Raymond set the pattern…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for balanced coverage across beats, abundant copy, and particular attention to important beats such as foreign affairs. Example: front pages crowded with foreign and local news and editors traveling abroad to secure firsthand coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of partisan 'isms' and eccentric doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Raymond sought a paper which, like the Tribune, should take a higher moral tone than the Herald or Sun, but which, unlike Greeley’s paper, should avoid 'isms' and eccentricities of doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an editorial stance that resists doctrinaire or eccentric ideological posturing; pursue broad appeal and a reputation for reasoned judgment rather than sectarian advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline construction: multi-deck 'label' heads; avoid verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mexican war news brought in the common use of headlines in multiple decks … Verbs were generally avoided, and each deck was a ‘label’ head.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stacked multi-deck headlines for big stories; compose short, noun/phrase-style 'label' decks rather than verb-centered sentences. For very large stories, extend heads vertically and add additional decks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead style: editorialized leads vs factual leads
rubrics_metrics.description: “News leads were often editorial comment, or they consisted of information about how the story had been received… In the fifties, however, there was a noticeable tendency to abandon this type of editorialized lead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that 19th-century practice often led with editorial comment; the emerging best practice was to move toward more factual, direct leads that present facts early rather than long editorializing. The Baltimore Sun example shows long, reception-oriented leads as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustration constrained by cost and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: “There were rare examples of illustration by means of woodcuts… wood engraving was expensive and the process was too slow for timely news illustration; thus the Herald’s pictures … were printed two weeks after the event.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve illustrations for special occasions; understand that cuts/engravings are costly and slow, often unsuitable for breaking news. Maps or portraits might appear occasionally but are not reliable for timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page size and 'blanket sheet' competition
rubrics_metrics.description: “With the advent of cylinder presses, it had become possible to print large sheets; and page sizes began to grow larger… there developed a curious competition for size… The largest size reached for regular daily publication was … eleven wide columns on a page measuring about 3x5 feet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper size and column count were competitive features — larger pages could signal prestige; penny papers remained small to keep price low while larger (blanket) sheets used size to contrast with cheap competitors. Choose size strategically according to market positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial page as a distinct department and its content
rubrics_metrics.description: “The editorial page as a department of the newspaper came into general acceptance… From one to four columns of editorials, often preceded by a column summary of important news, shared the page with a Washington letter, book reviews, and other material.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a coherent editorial page with multiple columns of commentary, summaries, and regular features (Washington letter, reviews). The page should discuss political, social, economic, and literary topics in an adequate literary style and aim high — news and editorial were not yet fully divorced, so blending informative editorial and news summary was common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/weekly paper focus: politics and boosterism
rubrics_metrics.description: “These pioneer towns all wanted and secured newspapers for both promotional and political reasons. In the first place they wanted them as 'boosters'… they were politically minded, and they wanted newspapers in order to promote the spread of their favorite partisan doctrine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that small-town weeklies often functioned as boosters and partisan organs; they were expected to promote local growth and national political positions, and might even be denominational or missionary organs. Editorial content should serve these local/promotional/political functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and distribution: use of rail, telegraph, steamers, pony express
rubrics_metrics.description: “The railroads and telegraph had covered the country… Eastern papers fed special California editions… The Overland Stage … made no better time than the steamboats… Two years later came the famous pony express, carrying two mails a week, and making the trip in half the time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize methods that improve timeliness of news (telegraph, rail, express lines). For distant markets, consider special regional editions; timely delivery is a competitive advantage and affects pricing and circulation (e.g., California editions sold high on arrival).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and capital requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: “The new company was capitalized at $100,000, half of which was required for the mechanical plant… its expenses were likewise enormous for those days— $78,000 for its first year, more than half of that going for print-paper.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful newspaper ventures require sufficient capitalization for presses and materials; operating costs (especially paper) can be a major expense. Pricing, additional investment, or selling stock may be necessary before reaching a paying basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-gathering quality: use of competent correspondents and firsthand reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: “In his desire for adequate foreign news, Raymond himself went to Italy to cover the war of 1859… he distinguished himself there as a capable war correspondent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value firsthand, on-the-ground reporting and send capable correspondents to cover important events (e.g., wars, foreign affairs); such coverage raises a paper’s reputation and provides substantive material for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and pagination strategy for circulation growth
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was unusually well edited… In ten weeks it had leaped to 20,000 circulation… it was therefore forced … to increase its subscription price to two cents… When it doubled its price it also doubled its number of pages; and by 1860 it was not far behind the Tribune in circulation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance price and content volume: a low price (penny press) can drive rapid circulation but may be unsustainable without page count adjustments or price increases; doubling price can be accompanied by increased page count to retain readers while improving revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial advocacy and political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Joseph Medill is best remembered as a chief editorial advocate of Lincoln… He and his partner… built up the Lincoln ‘boom’ with a zeal and political sagacity…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial pages can actively shape public opinion and political outcomes; editors may use the paper to promote candidates/policies. Recognize the power and responsibility of editorial advocacy as a dimension of a paper's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editioning for distant markets (special regional editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Eastern papers fed special California editions to the news-hungry forty-niners… the Tribune, Herald, and Evening Post each sent out from New York about 10,000 copies of its California edition by monthly steamers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For far-flung readerships, produce special regional or overseas editions timed to transport schedules; be mindful that transit delays reduce freshness but can still be commercially valuable if tailored to audience demand.
